title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Behaviour for Temporally Structured Crime-Count Prediction
content: Predicting crime counts is a difficult technology problem because the data are temporally dependent, uneven across locations and categories, vulnerable to leakage, and often dominated by persistence from prior periods. This study evaluates how distinct machine-learning (ML) regression families behave when applied to temporally structured crime-count data and asks whether increased model complexity produces measurable improvements over a simple seasonal benchmark. This study evaluates five ML regression families - Random Forest Model (RFM), Extreme Gradient Boosting Regressor (XGBR), K-Nearest Neighbor Regressor (KNNR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Multi-Layer Perceptron Regressor (MLPR) - compared across alternative categorical encoding scenarios (S), while Seasonal Naïve (SNa-ïve) prediction was retained as a transparent benchmark. The experimental protocol used rolling-origin tuning over  2019–2023, a separate 2024 validation period, and a one-pass 2025 held-out comparative evaluation of frozen candidate configurations. The 2025 observations were not used to define features, preprocessing rules, encoding scenarios, hyperparameter grids, or tuned   hyperparameters. Because the trained configuration used for the later forecasting demonstration was chosen after inspection of the 2025 comparison, the 2025 scores are treated as comparative evidence across pre-specified candidates rather than as an independent post-selection validation of that forecasting choice. SNaïve achieved the lowest 2025 error (RMSE=44.162; MAE=21.224; R²=0.9669). Among the trained candidates, XGBR S4 had the lowest RMSE (56.449), followed closely by RFM S4 (57.088). Encoding choice affected trained-model behaviour, prediction intervals showed mild undercoverage, local error varied substantially, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis showed that the one-year same-quarter lag was the dominant explanatory feature. The 2026–2027 values are unvalidated model projections and are not findings about future crime outcomes. The paper therefore reports a bounded empirical           comparison and reproducible temporal evaluation protocol for this administrative crime-count dataset; it does not claim universal crime prediction, hotspot detection, or a general operational  decision rule.
